issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically to stop thinking about a single mugging/robbery is clinically possible but is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile because there are no memory/intrusion items, no trigger-linked re-experiencing pattern, and the formulation leaves Triggers and Memory inactive. This strategy addresses a symptom pattern not otherwise represented in the selected items.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is not impossible, but for a mugging/robbery it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile. The other items emphasize hyperarousal, threat sensitivity, institutional betrayal, and numbing; this culturally/community-focused appraisal is not clearly linked to those features or to the formulation's active appraisal-threat-strategy loop, making it the least coherent appraisal item in this set.

vignette:
Marisol García was a 53-year-old Latin American woman who had spent most of her adult life in New York building a demanding career as a stock broker, a role that required her to move quickly between clients, phone calls, and the constant noise of the trading floor and city streets. Before the robbery, she had prided herself on being composed, efficient, and hard to rattle. The mugging happened on an ordinary worknight, after she left the office later than usual and walked toward her car with her bag tucked close under her arm. On a street that she had used countless times, two men came up from behind so abruptly that she barely had time to turn. One movement was enough to make her freeze; then one of them shoved her, demanded her bag, and reached toward her so fast that she could only think in fragments. She remembered the hard, metallic flash of fear, the way her body seemed to know before her mind could catch up that she was not in control, and the humiliating certainty that no one was coming to help. When it was over, she got home shaken and ashamed, replaying every second and feeling furious that the people and systems that were supposed to make a city feel safe had not protected her.

In the weeks that followed, Marisol noticed that she was no longer moving through the world in the same way. On the street and in parking lots she scanned constantly, her eyes catching on alleyways, parked cars, and any cluster of people who looked as if they might turn toward her. Sudden movements by others put her immediately on guard: if a stranger pivoted too quickly near her desk, or if someone came up beside her unexpectedly in the elevator at her office building, her whole body tightened before she could tell herself it was nothing. Ordinary sounds that used to blend into the background—a door slamming, a phone dropping, a laugh that burst out too sharply—made her jump. At work, where she had once felt confident taking meetings in glass-walled conference rooms and walking to lunch by herself, she found herself choosing routes and seating with unusual care, sitting near exits and watching who was behind her when she crossed the lobby. She did not describe these choices as fear so much as necessity; in her mind, the world had become a place where danger could appear without warning and where being unprepared meant being caught again.

Marisol also began to rely on habits that felt, to her, like ways of keeping bad luck at bay. Before leaving home she found herself checking and rechecking locks, then silently rehearsing what she would do if she heard footsteps behind her. She would sometimes repeat small mental phrases to herself before walking out into the street or stepping into the garage, as if saying the right words or arranging her thoughts correctly might prevent another attack. She knew these rituals were not logical, but they brought a temporary sense of control, and she was reluctant to abandon them. When she felt even mildly threatened, she became overly compliant, quick to agree, quick to smile, quick to hand over her bag or her seat if anyone seemed impatient. She found herself apologizing more than she used to, as though making herself easy to deal with might keep attention away from her. At the office this showed up in subtle ways: she would accept last-minute demands without protest, let colleagues step ahead of her, and keep her own discomfort private, because part of her believed that being agreeable was safer than being noticed.

As the months went on, Marisol’s view of herself and of the world grew darker. She was no longer able to think of her city as merely busy or stressful; in her mind, it was dangerous in a deeper, more fundamental way. She felt let down by the institutions and routines that were supposed to protect ordinary people, and that sense of betrayal stayed with her. Even in moments when nothing was happening, she described feeling dead inside, as if some part of her had gone flat after the robbery and had not returned. Her husband noticed that she was quieter at home, less responsive than before, and that she often sat rigidly in the living room while her gaze drifted toward the windows and door. Marisol herself said that she did not feel like the same woman who used to move through her days with confidence. She was functioning, going to work, returning home, keeping her life in order, but every outing required vigilance, and every unexpected noise or movement pulled her back into the same hard, immediate alertness.

By the time she sought help, it was not because she believed the danger had passed, but because she was exhausted by living as if it never had. Her symptoms had reached a point of interfering with her sense of safety at work and in everyday errands, and she was tired of feeling on edge in places that used to be familiar. What frightened her most was the thought that she would never again trust the world—or her own body—to let her relax. What she hoped for, though she said it carefully, was to feel present with her husband, to walk into her office without bracing for impact, and to stop living as if another attack were waiting just around the corner.
